title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every episode: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change outcomes by invoking a validator‑triggered repair; because every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation, no repairs were invoked and the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, exact numeric outcomes, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired result, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe, ordered device configurations is a core NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize candidate configurations, but textual fidelity does not imply operational safety: ordering errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑resource touches produce harmful applies in real networks. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are applied in an emulator and deterministically scored—exposes these semantic failure modes and supports operationally meaningful metrics [1].

A widely proposed mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are found [2,3]. Prior work demonstrates promise for GVR on many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about empirical verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and about experiment designs that reliably produce informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [1,2,3].

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to measure a precisely defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. Our contributions are (1) an artifact‑grounded execution and analysis of this preregistered paired GVR test (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) direct mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact verified numeric outcomes; and (3) an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and recommendations for future informative designs.
sections.related_work:
Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena is a recent example of an executable closed‑loop benchmark [1]. Work on automatic configuration repair shows generate–validate patterns and high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults under particular assumptions [2]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions for safe NetOps automation [3,4]. The engineering evolution of configuration analysis tools such as Batfish provides precedent for scalable verifier design and incremental verification [5].

Our study differs by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (explicitly constraining paired generation), emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and full archival of per‑call traces and validator traces enabling exact reconciliation of the reported estimand to archived artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis mapping and bootstrap parameters are archived in the execution bundle; the primary analysis executor produced the paired contingency table and bootstrap CI per the preregistration.

Design and generation semantics: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the system produced exactly one shared initial LLM generation per task and both arms used that same generation. Under this contract a paired difference can arise only if the shared candidate fails deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair changes the guarded final output. The preregistered adapter allowed up to one repair call per guarded episode.

Tasks and sampling: N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks, blocked into topology/vendor clusters, composed as in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Tasks were generated deterministically and include intent payloads, initial states, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints; representative task manifests are archived.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution declared model gpt-5-mini and used a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The adapter family implemented the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and constrained repair budget to at most one validator‑triggered repair per guarded episode.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator+validator assigned a binary final outcome (safe vs unsafe) based on semantic invariant checks. Predeclared exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures after the preregistered retry policy; the run encountered no such exclusions. Missingness and exclusion counts are reported in the archived analysis summary.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed per plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. The execution call audit shows exactly one initial model call per task (hosted model calls = 240) consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Task difficulty composition: Observed difficulty labels recorded across tasks were: "very_hard" = 192 tasks (80.0%) and "extreme" = 48 tasks (20.0%).

Primary binary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0. The paired contingency is n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All numeric analysis outputs and CSV artifacts are archived and traceable to the registered analysis executor outputs.

Validator activity and repair utilization: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0). Validator traces recorded final_state snapshots, required_command_count, and per‑task validity flags; for every task the shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation, hence the guarded path produced the same final configuration as the baseline for every pair. Planned sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures were unused because no items met those flagging criteria.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only alter paired outcomes by applying a validator‑triggered repair or when the shared candidate failed validation. In this execution every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked, so the guarded and baseline final configurations were identical for all pairs—mechanistically producing the observed degenerate contingency (estimate = 0.0, CI = [0.0, 0.0], p = 1.0).

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces the model‑call budget and ensures a direct pairing of the same LLM sample, but it also removes generator variability between arms; therefore, observing verifier benefit under this contract requires initial candidates that violate the verifier checks. To obtain informative paired contrasts in future studies one should: (A) permit independent initial generations per arm; (B) increase adversary strength or inject controlled generator perturbations to create validator failures; and/or (C) expand repair budgets and repair‑search strategies to exercise the repair mechanism. These recommendations follow directly from the execution audit and validator traces showing identical shared initial responses and zero repair usage.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit, preregistered design choice that limits causal contrast interpretation. Construct validity: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of semantic checks; passing the verifier does not guarantee absence of all conceivable semantic faults. External validity: tasks were drawn from an emulation‑grounded synthetic corpus; extrapolation to production multi‑vendor deployments requires caution. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detecting verifier benefit in this design; future power analyses should account for generation variability and adversary strength to ensure informative discordant pairs.

Practical takeaway: The artifact archive documents a clean, preregistered execution where contractual semantics determined the possible paired contrasts. Future GVR evaluations intended to estimate verifier causal effects should avoid contracts that eliminate generator variability between arms or should intentionally create validation failures that allow the repair machinery to demonstrate value.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only differ from baseline when the single shared initial candidate failed validation or when a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run all shared candidates passed and no repairs were invoked, producing the degenerate paired outcome. The archived artifacts and analysis outputs fully support these findings and point to concrete experimental changes—generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budgets—that are needed for informative future causal evaluations of verifier benefit in GVR pipelines.

disclosure_statement: Model and orchestration: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting reported here were performed autonomously after the lock. Generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore only validator failures of the shared candidate or validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences. Archive pointer: the full execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the evidence bundle. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
